title: Come and See
subtitle: Selected passages from the Gospel of John
source: Text drawn from the King James Version (1611, public domain). Editorial framing by the editors of Purify.

sections.title: The call of Philip
sections.framing: Philip was a Galilean of Bethsaida, the same town as Andrew and Peter. The Fourth Gospel tells of his call on the day after Andrew brought his brother, and lays beside Philip's own call the words by which he in turn brought Nathanael. The pattern is the Gospel's quiet method of the first weeks: one disciple finds another, and the witness travels from mouth to mouth before any public preaching has begun.
paragraphs: The day following Jesus would go forth into Galilee, and findeth Philip, and saith unto him, Follow me.
Now Philip was of Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.
Philip findeth Nathanael, and saith unto him, We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, did write, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.
And Nathanael said unto him, Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth? Philip saith unto him, Come and see.
notes: 'Come and see' is Philip's answer to Nathanael's skepticism, and is the same invitation the Lord had used to Andrew and his companion the day before (John 1:39). The Fathers note that the Gospel passes from teacher to disciple to brother in those same three words.
Philip is to be distinguished from Philip the Deacon and Evangelist (Acts 6, 8), who was one of the Seven and the father of the four prophesying daughters.

sections.title: Lord, shew us the Father
sections.framing: On the night of the Mystical Supper, after the Lord had spoken of going to prepare a place and of being himself the way, Philip put a request that was the whole hope of the patriarchs of Israel: to see the Father, even for an instant, as Moses had asked on Sinai. The Lord's answer is one of the central sayings of the Fourth Gospel on the unity of the Father and the Son.
paragraphs: Philip saith unto him, Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us.
Jesus saith unto him, Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou then, Shew us the Father?
notes: St. Athanasius cites this verse repeatedly in the Four Discourses Against the Arians as a foundation text for the consubstantiality of the Son with the Father.

Tradition relates that after Pentecost Philip preached the Gospel in Phrygia, in Lydia, and at Hierapolis, where he was crucified head-downward together with the Apostle Bartholomew and his own sister Mariamne. His feast is kept on the fourteenth of November, and he is named the head of the Nativity Fast that begins the following day.
